name: Flutamide

angle.text: Flutamide is a prostate-cancer antiandrogen that some hair-loss communities discuss, in topical or oral form, as an off-label way to curb androgen-driven thinning and keep more hair. Its use for hair has been studied mainly in women, and forum comparisons with other antiandrogens rest on anecdote.

summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen sometimes used off-label for female hirsutism and hair loss; liver toxicity makes it a last-line choice.
note: Boxed warning for liver failure; label says it is for men only.
currentQuick:
Flutamide is a prescription antiandrogen approved for prostate cancer. It has also been used off-label in women for excess hair growth, acne and hair thinning.
Evidence for scalp hair is thin, and guidelines rank it behind other antiandrogens because of liver risk.
How it works: It blocks androgen receptors, so testosterone and DHT have less effect on follicles and oil glands.
Risks and caveats: Boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal liver injury; also fetal toxicity, methemoglobinemia, hot flashes and sexual side effects in men.
deepLead:
Flutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that blocks the androgen receptor. It was the first drug of its type approved in the US, in 1989, for prostate cancer, and its labelled use is in combination with an LHRH agonist for locally confined and metastatic prostate carcinoma . Its label carries a boxed warning for liver injury and says it is for use only in men .
Off-label, flutamide has been used in women for hirsutism, acne and female pattern hair loss, and discussed in androgen-focused forum circles as a hair-related antiandrogen . A French review of antiandrogen treatments placed flutamide as third-line therapy for severe hirsutism in women, noting no market authorisation for that use . Published evidence for scalp hair loss is limited; a 2023 AGA review noted only finasteride and minoxidil are FDA-approved for androgenetic alopecia .

name: Bicalutamide

angle.text: Bicalutamide is a prostate-cancer antiandrogen used off-label for female pattern hair loss, and some forum users also float it for recovery after finasteride or isotretinoin. Evidence for hair is retrospective data in women; the recovery idea is based on anecdote.

summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen used off-label for women's hair loss; supported by retrospective data only and with a liver-injury warning.
note: Label warns of severe liver injury; hair use is off-label.
currentQuick:
Bicalutamide is a prescription antiandrogen for prostate cancer. Dermatologists sometimes prescribe low doses off-label for female pattern hair loss and excess hair.
Evidence comes from reviews and retrospective data rather than randomised trials, and it has little presence in looksmaxxing forums.
How it works: It binds the androgen receptor and blocks testosterone and DHT from activating it, reducing androgen effects on hair follicles.
Risks and caveats: The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury and requires liver testing. Hot flashes, fatigue and other effects are common in cancer patients; off-label users report liver enzyme elevation.
deepLead:
Bicalutamide (brand name Casodex) is a nonsteroidal androgen-receptor antagonist. Its US label indicates the 50 mg dose in combination with an LHRH analogue for stage D2 metastatic prostate cancer, and states that 150 mg daily is not approved alone or with other treatments in the US .
Outside that indication, bicalutamide has been used off-label for female pattern hair loss and hirsutism, and in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women . A 2025 review describes it as of recent interest in female pattern hair loss, and notes off-label use to improve Sinclair grading . A systematic review of injectable therapies for androgenetic alopecia (AGA) lists bicalutamide among agents studied in mesotherapy .
The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury . Forum discussion in the sources is limited: T Nation members have mentioned bicalutamide in androgen-receptor and post-isotretinoin recovery threads .

name: Cyproterone acetate

angle.text: Cyproterone acetate is a progestin-antiandrogen prescribed to women for hirsutism, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss, so it comes up in discussions of hormone-driven skin and hair. Its use for these conditions is established in clinical practice; appearance use in men is largely anecdotal.

summary: A progestin-antiandrogen used in women for hirsutism, acne and hair loss; effective in the clinic but limited by meningioma and liver risks.
note: Dose-dependent meningioma and liver toxicity risk; hair use is in women with hyperandrogenism.
currentQuick:
Cyproterone acetate is a prescription hormone drug that blocks androgens. Doctors use it, often with an estrogen pill, for excess hair growth, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss in women, and for prostate cancer and sexual-drive reduction in men.
Reviews rank it among first-line choices for hirsutism, but it is hardly discussed in looksmaxxing forums.
How it works: It blocks androgen receptors and acts as a progestin, lowering the brain signals that drive testosterone and estradiol production.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include meningioma at higher cumulative doses, liver toxicity, and thrombosis risk when combined with estrogen pills. Regulators restrict long-term high-dose use.
deepLead:
Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a synthetic steroidal antiandrogen and progestin. It blocks androgen receptors and, through its progestogenic action, suppresses gonadotropin release and so lowers testosterone production in men and estradiol in women . It is used for palliation in advanced prostate cancer, for hirsutism and severe acne in women (often with ethinylestradiol), and to reduce sexual drive in men with paraphilias .
In hair and appearance contexts, CPA is relevant to female pattern hair loss and hirsutism. A Dutch review described spironolactone or cyproterone acetate combined with an oral contraceptive as the safest and most effective approach for hirsutism in women with PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism . Its use is limited in many regions by a dose-dependent risk of meningioma and liver toxicity reported in a general reference .
Sources for this entry contain very little community discussion; mentions on T Nation are brief .

name: Latanoprost

angle.text: Latanoprost is a glaucoma eye drop whose side effects include longer, thicker lashes and darker iris pigmentation, which is why appearance communities mention it for lashes and eye colour. The effects are documented as side effects of the medical use; cosmetic trials have not been run.

summary: A glaucoma eye drop whose lash-lengthening and eye-darkening side effects get it mentioned in appearance circles; no cosmetic trials exist.
note: Iris darkening is listed as likely permanent on the label; not approved for cosmetic use.
currentQuick:
Latanoprost is a prescription eye drop for glaucoma and raised eye pressure. Its label lists longer, thicker, darker eyelashes and darker eyelid skin and irises among its effects.
Looksmaxxing discussion is sparse and mostly about eye darkening. No trial has tested it for cosmetic purposes; a Phase 1/2 trial pairing it with laser in alopecia areata is registered.
How it works: It is a prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue that increases fluid drainage from the eye through the uveoscleral pathway, lowering pressure. Pigment and lash changes are tissue effects of the same drug class.
Risks and caveats: Label warnings include permanent iris pigmentation, eyelid darkening, inflammation and macular oedema. A case report describes skin depigmentation. It is prescription-only and not approved for cosmetic use.
deepLead:
Latanoprost is a synthetic prostaglandin F2-alpha analogue applied as an ophthalmic solution to lower raised intraocular pressure (IOP) in open-angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. The US label describes its main action as increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour. It is a prescription medicine, and its approved use is medical rather than cosmetic.
Its relevance to appearance comes from side effects listed on its label: increased length, thickness, pigmentation and number of eyelashes, darkening of eyelid skin, and permanent darkening of the iris. Related prostaglandin analogues, notably bimatoprost, have been developed specifically for eyelash growth, and latanoprost is discussed by some users in the same context. A registered Phase 1/2 trial has also listed latanoprost combined with fractional laser for alopecia areata.
No published trial in the sources reviewed tests latanoprost as a cosmetic eyelash or eye-colour treatment. Evidence for its eyelash effect comes from its glaucoma trials and label, and community discussion of eye darkening is largely anecdotal and often framed as a curiosity.

name: Onion juice

angle.text: Onion juice is a folk scalp remedy that users apply hoping to regrow hair and thicken thinning areas, often mentioned alongside rosemary oil and rice water. Evidence for this use is one small trial in alopecia areata plus anecdote, rather than trials in pattern baldness.

summary: A folk scalp remedy with one small alopecia areata trial behind it and reviews calling the evidence limited.
note: Evidence is a single small 2002 trial plus reviews noting design limits; no large trials.
currentQuick:
Onion juice is pressed from onion bulbs and applied to the scalp as a natural hair-regrowth remedy. It circulates in social-media hair-loss advice alongside rosemary oil and rice water.
A 2002 controlled trial in alopecia areata reported more regrowth than tap water. Reviews describe the evidence base as small and limited.
How it works: Proposed mechanisms in the literature are not established for onion juice specifically; reviews of herbal remedies cite ideas such as antioxidant effects and improved circulation as general explanations.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed report no specific safety data for scalp use. It is an unregulated food-derived preparation, and reviews advise further study.
deepLead:
Onion juice is the liquid pressed from the bulb of the common onion (Allium cepa), applied to the scalp as a folk remedy for hair loss and to encourage hair growth. It is discussed in reviews of social-media hair-loss advice alongside rosemary oil, rice water and garlic gel.
The best-known clinical evidence is a small 2002 controlled trial in patchy alopecia areata, in which participants applying crude onion juice twice daily for two months were reported to show more regrowth than those applying tap water. Narrative reviews describe the wider literature as limited by small samples, lack of comparison with standard treatments, and conflicts of interest, and note that onion juice has mostly been studied in combination products. A 2025 review of online alopecia misinformation lists onion juice among the unproven natural remedies promoted online.

name: Rosemary oil

angle.text: Rosemary oil is used as a natural alternative to minoxidil, applied to the scalp and sometimes to brows and lashes for thicker growth. One small 2015 trial compared it with 2% minoxidil for pattern hair loss; the brow and lash uses rest on anecdote.

summary: The natural minoxidil alternative: one small 2015 trial matched 2% minoxidil, but reviews call the evidence thin and a Canadian consensus did not recommend it.
note: Essential oil; evidence rests largely on one 100-person trial.
currentQuick:
Rosemary oil is a plant essential oil applied to the scalp (and sometimes brows) as a natural hair-growth aid. It is popular as a minoxidil alternative.
A 2015 trial of 100 people found similar hair-count gains to 2% minoxidil after six months. Reviews describe the evidence as limited, and a 2025 Canadian consensus did not recommend it.
How it works: Proposed explanations include improved microcirculation, and some forum users suggest effects on gene expression; neither is established for hair growth in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Reviews describe a minimal side-effect profile; the 2015 trial reported scalp itching less often than with minoxidil per Grokipedia. It is sold as a cosmetic or aromatherapy product rather than an approved hair-loss drug.
deepLead:
Rosemary oil is the essential oil steam-distilled from the leaves of the rosemary plant (Salvia rosmarinus, formerly Rosmarinus officinalis), long used in traditional medicine and cooking. In appearance communities it is applied to the scalp, and sometimes to eyebrows and lashes, as a natural hair-growth treatment and is frequently described as an alternative to minoxidil.
The main clinical evidence is a 2015 randomised trial of 100 people with androgenetic alopecia comparing rosemary oil with 2% minoxidil for six months; hair counts rose significantly in both groups from baseline with no significant difference between them. Reviews generally count rosemary oil among natural products that may be considered, while stressing the small number and limited quality of studies. A 2025 Canadian consensus statement of eleven physicians listed rosemary oil among interventions it did not recommend for androgenetic alopecia.

name: Anastrozole

angle.text: Anastrozole is a breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers discuss as a way to delay growth-plate closure and add height, and that TRT users discuss for oestrogen control. The height theory is untested in healthy people; its approved use is in breast cancer.

summary: A breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers and TRT users discuss for oestrogen control; no trials show a height gain in healthy people.
note: Label warns of bone loss and cardiovascular events; off-label use for height in adolescents is untested.
currentQuick:
Anastrozole (Arimidex) is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for breast cancer in postmenopausal women. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed for delaying growth-plate closure to gain height, and for oestrogen control during testosterone use.
No controlled trial shows it increases height in healthy adolescents; a gynecomastia review says it has not been consistently useful in boys.
How it works: It blocks aromatase, the enzyme converting testosterone and androstenedione to oestrogen, lowering oestradiol. Oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, which is the basis of height-related interest.
Risks and caveats: The label lists reduced bone density, higher cholesterol, cardiovascular events in women with heart disease and fetal harm. Forum users report fatigue and crashed oestrogen. Prescription-only; its use for height is off-label.
deepLead:
Anastrozole, sold as Arimidex among other names, is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. Its approved uses are in postmenopausal women with hormone receptor-positive breast cancer, where it lowers oestrogen by blocking the aromatase enzyme. It is a prescription medicine.
In bodybuilding and testosterone-therapy settings it is used to manage oestrogen, and on looksmax.org it is discussed by users, including self-described teenagers, who hope to delay growth-plate closure and increase adult height, often alongside growth hormone. Published research on aromatase inhibitors for height or for gynecomastia in healthy males is limited; a 2023 review of gynecomastia in boys says anastrozole and letrozole have not been consistently useful in that age group.
Documented adverse effects from the US label include reduced bone mineral density, raised cholesterol and ischaemic cardiovascular events in women with prior heart disease, and possible fetal harm. Looksmaxxing use for height is off-label and, for adolescents, is not an approved indication.

name: Letrozole

angle.text: Letrozole is a potent aromatase inhibitor that heightmaxxers consider for delaying growth plates, and that some users link to leanness through lowered oestrogen. Trials cover breast cancer and fertility; use for height or gains in healthy people is untested and discussed mostly on forums.

summary: A potent breast-cancer and fertility aromatase inhibitor that heightmaxxers eye for delaying growth plates; no trials in healthy teens, and forums warn of crashed oestrogen.
note: Label warns of bone loss and fetal harm; use for height is off-label and untested in adolescents.
currentQuick:
Letrozole is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer, also used in fertility treatment. Looksmax.org users, including teenagers, discuss it for delaying growth-plate closure to add height.
No controlled trial in healthy adolescents was found; forum users themselves warn it is the strongest option and can crash oestrogen.
How it works: It blocks the aromatase enzyme, lowering conversion of androgens to oestrogen. Since oestrogen drives growth-plate fusion, the hope is a longer growth window.
Risks and caveats: The label lists bone density loss, raised cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, hot flashes and joint pain, and it can cause fetal harm. Prescription-only; height use is off-label.
deepLead:
Letrozole is a non-steroidal aromatase inhibitor taken by mouth. The US label lists adjuvant and extended adjuvant treatment of hormone receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women, and first- and second-line treatment of advanced disease. It is also widely used in fertility medicine for ovulation induction.
On looksmax.org it is discussed mainly for heightmaxxing, by users who hope to delay growth-plate closure by lowering oestrogen, often together with growth hormone or MK-677, and some of whom describe themselves as 15 or 16 years old. Users compare it with anastrozole and exemestane, and several describe it as the most potent and the most likely to crash oestrogen. No controlled trial in healthy adolescents testing letrozole for adult height was found in the sources reviewed.
The label warns of decreased bone mineral density, increased cholesterol, fatigue and dizziness, and embryo-fetal toxicity; it is contraindicated in pregnancy. It is a prescription medicine.

name: Exemestane

angle.text: Exemestane is a steroidal aromatase inhibitor that teen heightmaxxers favour as the milder option for keeping growth plates open and adding height. It is approved for breast cancer; the height use has not been tested in healthy adolescents and rests on forum reports.

summary: A steroidal breast-cancer aromatase inhibitor teen heightmaxxers favour as the 'milder' option; no trials in healthy adolescents.
note: Label warns of bone density loss and fetal harm; height use is off-label and untested.
currentQuick:
Exemestane (Aromasin) is a prescription aromatase inhibitor for postmenopausal breast cancer. On looksmax.org, mostly teenagers discuss it for keeping growth plates open and adding height, often with growth hormone.
No trial has tested this in healthy adolescents. Users debate it against anastrozole and letrozole.
How it works: It irreversibly inactivates aromatase, reducing oestrogen production, and is a steroid structurally related to androstenedione. Lower oestrogen is thought to delay growth-plate fusion.
Risks and caveats: The label lists bone density loss, hot flushes, fatigue, joint pain and fetal harm; a maculopathy report exists. Forum users report hair and hormone problems. Prescription-only; height use is off-label.
deepLead:
Exemestane, sold as Aromasin, is an oral steroidal aromatase inhibitor that irreversibly inactivates the aromatase enzyme. The US label indicates it for adjuvant treatment of oestrogen-receptor-positive early breast cancer in postmenopausal women after two to three years of tamoxifen, and for advanced breast cancer progressing after tamoxifen. It is a prescription medicine.
On looksmax.org it is discussed, often by self-described 15-year-olds, as an option to keep growth plates open for height gain, frequently alongside growth hormone, and as an alternative to anastrozole and letrozole. Some users describe it as milder and as having androgenic properties; others report hair or hormonal problems. No published trial in healthy adolescents testing exemestane for height or other appearance outcomes was found.
Label warnings include reductions in bone mineral density over time and fetal harm. Case literature also describes bilateral maculopathy associated with exemestane.

name: Tamoxifen

angle.text: Tamoxifen is a breast-cancer SERM that bodybuilders and TRT users take to treat or prevent gynecomastia and sometimes to support muscle gain. It is used clinically for breast conditions and has been studied for male gynecomastia; the muscle-gain claims are based on anecdote.

summary: A breast-cancer SERM that bodybuilders and TRT users take for gynecomastia; label carries a boxed warning and nothing tests it for looks.
note: Boxed warning for uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism; appearance uses are off-label.
currentQuick:
Tamoxifen (Nolvadex) is a prescription oestrogen-receptor blocker for breast cancer. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding circles it is used off-label for gynecomastia and oestrogen control during steroid use, and some ask about growth-plate effects.
A review says it has been tried successfully in adolescent gynecomastia; no trials address its other cosmetic uses.
How it works: It binds oestrogen receptors, blocking oestrogen's effect in breast tissue while acting like oestrogen in other tissues such as bone and endometrium.
Risks and caveats: The US label's boxed warning covers uterine cancers, stroke and pulmonary embolism; it also lists liver effects, hot flashes and fetal harm. Retinopathy and low platelets have been reported. Prescription-only.
deepLead:
Tamoxifen, sold under the brand name Nolvadex among others, is a selective estrogen receptor modulator (SERM) taken by mouth. It acts as an oestrogen antagonist in breast tissue and as an agonist in some other tissues. The US label (for the oral solution Soltamox) lists treatment of metastatic breast cancer, adjuvant treatment of early-stage ER-positive breast cancer, reduction of risk after DCIS surgery, and risk reduction in high-risk women.
In appearance and bodybuilding settings it is used off-label, mostly to address gynecomastia and to manage oestrogen effects during or after anabolic steroid use. Looksmax.org users also ask whether SERMs affect growth-plate closure, with threads citing conflicting laboratory findings.
The US label carries a boxed warning for uterine malignancies, stroke and pulmonary embolism in the oncology setting, and warns of fetal harm and liver effects. It is a prescription medicine.

name: Clomiphene

angle.text: Clomiphene is a fertility SERM that men use off-label to raise their own testosterone without injections, or to recover after steroid cycles, in pursuit of more muscle and leanness. It has some evidence in hypogonadal men; effects on looks are untested.

summary: A fertility SERM that men use off-label to lift their own testosterone; some evidence in hypogonadal men, none for looks.
note: Label warns of possibly irreversible visual disturbances; male use is off-label.
currentQuick:
Clomiphene (Clomid) is a prescription drug for ovulation induction in women. Men use it off-label to raise their own testosterone, and looksmax.org discusses it for 'tmaxxing' and post-cycle recovery.
A 2022 review covers its use in hypogonadal men; no trials test it for cosmetic goals in healthy people.
How it works: It blocks oestrogen receptors in the brain's hypothalamus and pituitary, raising gonadotropins and prompting the testes to make more testosterone.
Risks and caveats: The label lists ovarian enlargement and flushes, plus visual disturbances that may be irreversible. Users report mood and libido changes. Prescription-only; teens asking for it without a prescription appear on forums.
deepLead:
Clomiphene citrate (Clomid) is a selective estrogen receptor modulator taken by mouth. The US label indicates it for ovulatory dysfunction in women desiring pregnancy, particularly polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS). In men it is used off-label for hypogonadism, where it aims to raise the body's own testosterone and preserve sperm production, in contrast to exogenous testosterone.
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities clomiphene is discussed under labels such as 'tmaxxing' and post-cycle therapy: users describe taking it to boost endogenous testosterone, and compare it with enclomiphene, one of its isomers, which one thread says boosted testosterone more with fewer side effects in a 2024 study. Several posters are teenagers asking how to obtain it without a prescription.
A 2022 systematic review of clomiphene in men with hypogonadism included 19 studies, four of them randomised, and assessed hormone levels, symptoms and safety. The label lists ovarian enlargement and vasomotor flushes as the most common adverse events and warns of visual symptoms that are usually reversible but may be irreversible.

name: Enclomiphene

angle.text: Enclomiphene is the trans-isomer of clomiphene, taken by men to lift natural testosterone while preserving fertility and testicle size, and sometimes discussed for post-cycle recovery or height. It has been studied in men with secondary hypogonadism; appearance and height uses are largely untested.

summary: The trans-isomer of clomiphene, studied for raising testosterone in men with secondary hypogonadism; forum use for appearance or height is largely untested.
note: Not approved by the FDA for any use; trials were in men with low testosterone, not for cosmetic or growth purposes.
currentQuick:
Enclomiphene is one of the two geometric isomers that make up clomiphene citrate, a drug long prescribed for female ovulatory dysfunction. It was developed as an oral treatment for men whose low testosterone stems from reduced pituitary signalling (secondary hypogonadism).
In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums it is discussed as a way to raise testosterone without injecting it, as a component of post-cycle protocols, and, in some threads, in relation to height or bone growth. Clinical trials exist for the hypogonadism use; none have tested it for appearance outcomes.
How it works: Enclomiphene blocks estrogen receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Reduced estrogen feedback is reported to raise luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH), which prompts the testes to make more testosterone themselves.
Risks and caveats: Published trials describe short-term safety comparable to placebo and testosterone gel, but long-term data are limited. Forum users report fatigue, mood effects and other complaints. Enclomiphene has no FDA approval, and products obtained outside prescriptions are of uncertain quality. Trial data in teenagers are absent.
deepLead:
Enclomiphene (also called trans-clomiphene; the citrate salt was developed under the name Androxal) is a non-steroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator that behaves mainly as an estrogen receptor antagonist. It is the trans-stereoisomer of clomiphene citrate, a drug widely prescribed for decades for ovulatory dysfunction in women .
Its main investigated use is in men with secondary hypogonadism, where it is reported to raise endogenous testosterone by increasing gonadotropins, while preserving sperm counts in trials that compared it with topical testosterone . A 2025 meta-analysis of randomized trials of clomiphene or enclomiphene reported higher total testosterone, LH and FSH than placebo, with considerable heterogeneity between studies .
In online appearance and physique communities, enclomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-raising option, as part of post-cycle or TRT-adjacent protocols, and by some posters in connection with height or bone growth. No published trial has tested it for those purposes, and it is not approved by regulators as a finished drug product.

name: Nicotine

angle.text: Nicotine, via pouches, gum or vapes, is used by some in appearance communities as an appetite suppressant to stay lean, and for focus. Trials have not tested it for leanness, and forum posters also debate effects on hair, skin and teeth.

summary: The stimulant and addictive alkaloid in tobacco and pouches, used by some in appearance communities as an appetite suppressant; no trials test it for leanness, and its documented harms are well established.
note: Highly addictive; raises heart rate and blood pressure. Approved nicotine products are labelled for smoking cessation, not weight loss.
currentQuick:
Nicotine is the main psychoactive alkaloid in tobacco. It is sold in cigarettes, vapes, oral pouches, gum, lozenges and patches. Regulated nicotine replacement products are marketed to reduce withdrawal and craving in people quitting smoking.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to suppress appetite and 'leanmaxx', and as a focus aid. Other posters describe it as harmful to looks, citing sleep, skin, teeth, hair and anxiety complaints. The cessation literature is large; the evidence for any appearance or fat-loss use specifically is thin.
How it works: Nicotine activates nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, prompting release of dopamine and other neurotransmitters. Forum posts attribute appetite suppression and higher energy expenditure to this action; those posts cite older physiological studies that are not evaluated in this article's sources.
Risks and caveats: Nicotine is addictive, raises heart rate and blood pressure, and the FDA-listed labels for nicotine gum caution people with heart disease and pregnant users. E-cigarettes and pouches have been studied for oral and other effects, with long-term data still accumulating. Forum users report insomnia, anxiety, palpitations and dependence.
deepLead:
Nicotine is a plant alkaloid found chiefly in the tobacco plant and is the principal addictive component of tobacco products. It acts on nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the nervous system and increases release of dopamine and other neurotransmitters . It was isolated in 1828 according to one encyclopedic summary .
Regulated nicotine products such as gum, lozenges and patches are used in nicotine replacement therapy to ease withdrawal during smoking cessation . The US label for nicotine polacrilex gum states that it reduces withdrawal symptoms, including craving, associated with quitting smoking, and warns that nicotine can raise heart rate and blood pressure .
In looksmaxxing communities, nicotine is discussed mainly as an appetite suppressant and stimulant for cutting body fat, with newer threads centred on oral pouches. Other community members argue that it harms appearance, and some report quitting as improving it. No clinical study found for this article has tested nicotine as an appearance or fat-loss intervention.

name: Benzoyl peroxide

angle.text: Benzoyl peroxide is the over-the-counter acne staple used in washes and leave-on products for clearer skin, and some users also use the wash on the body for breakouts and odor. Its acne use is backed by guidelines and decades of trials; the odor use is anecdotal.

summary: The over-the-counter acne staple with a strong guideline recommendation and decades of trials; the main trade-off is dryness and irritation.
note: Can irritate and dry skin, bleach fabric and hair, and is more irritating when combined with other topical actives.
currentQuick:
Benzoyl peroxide is a topical antibacterial and keratolytic agent sold in washes, creams and gels, mostly for acne. It is available over the counter in several strengths and is also found in prescription combinations with adapalene or clindamycin.
In the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline it receives a strong recommendation. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap acne product, and some posters also describe using it on the body to reduce odor, a use that has little published support in the published literature.
How it works: It releases oxygen radicals that act against Cutibacterium acnes, the skin bacterium involved in acne, and it has a peeling (keratolytic) effect that helps unclog pores.
Risks and caveats: Dryness, peeling, redness and stinging are the most commonly reported effects, and product labels advise that irritation is more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time. It can bleach fabric. Animal studies from 1981 reported tumour-promoting activity in mice under experimental conditions; the clinical relevance is not established in the published literature.
deepLead:
Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) is an organic peroxide used topically for acne vulgaris and sold over the counter in washes, creams, gels and leave-on products, as well as in prescription combination products . It acts as an antibacterial and keratolytic agent .
The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology guideline for acne management makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline . A JAMA review lists benzoyl peroxide among first-line topical therapies , and a 2022 network meta-analysis found a combined retinoid and benzoyl peroxide to be the most effective topical option for mild-to-moderate acne among those assessed .
In looksmaxxing communities, benzoyl peroxide is discussed as an inexpensive acne product, particularly during testosterone or steroid use, and some users promote it for reducing body odor . No trial found tests it for odor.

name: Snail mucin

angle.text: Snail mucin is a Korean-skincare staple used for hydration, a glowing look, fading acne marks and softening fine lines. Reviews describe small studies on hydration and scars as promising, with large clinical trials still lacking.

summary: The popular Korean-skincare ingredient made from snail secretion; reviews call it promising for hydration and scars but say large clinical trials are lacking.
note: Most published work is preclinical or small clinical studies; no formal toxicological monographs exist, and irritation or allergy is possible.
currentQuick:
Snail mucin, also called snail secretion filtrate, is the mucus of snails (often Cornu aspersum) used in serums, essences and creams, especially in Korean skincare. Its reported components include allantoin, glycolic acid, hyaluronic acid-type glycosaminoglycans, proteins and peptides.
Reviews describe uses in hydration, anti-aging, acne, scarring and hyperpigmentation, but say most studies are preclinical or small and call for larger trials. A 2022 randomized trial examined a serum with snail secretion filtrate in mask-related acne.
How it works: The proposed actions come from its mixture of ingredients: humectant and exfoliating compounds that may support hydration and surface smoothness, and proteins and peptides that cell and animal studies link with antimicrobial, antioxidant and wound-healing effects.
Risks and caveats: Reviews flag skin irritation, sensitisation and allergic reactions as possible, and note that standardised formulations and formal toxicology monographs are lacking. Product labels typically advise external use only and avoiding the eyes. A case report series on adolescents trying viral skincare trends is cited as a caution about social media skincare products generally.
deepLead:
Snail mucin, or snail secretion filtrate (SSF), is a mucus secretion of snails used as a cosmetic ingredient, particularly in Korean skincare . It has been described as a mixture containing allantoin, glycolic acid, proteins, glycosaminoglycans, enzymes, peptides and trace minerals .
Reviews list cosmetic uses including anti-aging, hydration, anti-acne, scarring and hyperpigmentation treatments, and medical research interest in antimicrobial, wound-healing, and drug-delivery applications. They also state that most studies have been preclinical or small clinical studies and call for larger trials .
Published studies did not include looksmaxxing forum discussion of snail mucin, so its place in those communities is not documented here.

name: Centella asiatica

angle.text: Centella asiatica, or cica, is used in calming Korean skincare products to reduce redness, help acne marks and scars heal, and support skin quality. Trials exist for wound and scar healing; evidence for anti-aging and general looks is small and mixed in quality.

summary: Gotu kola, the 'cica' plant behind many calming Korean skincare products; trials on wound and scar healing exist, but evidence for anti-aging or looks is small and mixed in quality.
note: Evidence is mainly wound healing, small trials and lab studies; cosmetic claims rest on limited human data.
currentQuick:
Centella asiatica is a creeping plant used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine and now widely used in skincare as 'cica'. Its active compounds are triterpenes such as asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid.
Reviews describe benefits for wound healing and scars, and there are small trials in aging skin and post-procedure recovery. Large, long trials on cosmetic outcomes are lacking in the published literature, and forums rarely discuss it for appearance.
How it works: In cell and animal studies, the triterpenes stimulate collagen I and growth factors involved in repair and reduce inflammatory markers such as IL-1 beta and IL-6. A systematic review of four clinical trials suggested it might enhance wound healing through improved angiogenesis.
Risks and caveats: The published literature give little safety detail; labels for topical or oral products carry the usual precautions. Oral use appears in trials in diabetes and cognition, which are outside appearance use. Dermatology reviews recommend further research on safety, dosing and standardisation.
deepLead:
Centella asiatica (gotu kola, Indian pennywort) is a herbaceous plant of the Apiaceae family used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine . Its principal active compounds are pentacyclic triterpenes: asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid .
In skincare it is used in creams, serums and masks (often marketed as 'cica') for soothing, wound healing, scar appearance and anti-aging . A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded that it might enhance wound healing, while noting the small evidence base .
Evidence for cosmetic outcomes such as wrinkles, skin quality or looks is limited to small studies; a 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included it among botanical agents .

name: Bakuchiol

angle.text: Bakuchiol is promoted as a plant-based retinol alternative for wrinkles, pigmentation and acne, favoured by people who find retinol irritating. A handful of small trials report retinol-like results with less irritation.

summary: A plant-derived 'retinol alternative' for wrinkles and pigmentation, with a handful of small trials suggesting retinol-like results and less irritation.
note: Few and small trials; head-to-head evidence against retinol is limited and mostly cosmetic-industry studies.
currentQuick:
Bakuchiol is a phenolic compound extracted mainly from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia (babchi), used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine. It has no structural similarity to retinoids, but has been marketed as a gentler functional alternative to retinol in anti-aging creams and serums.
A systematic review of dermatology studies found 16 preclinical and seven clinical studies, mostly on photoaging, acne and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, with results described as comparable to topical retinoids. Evidence base is small and not large-scale.
How it works: Gene-expression studies reported that bakuchiol regulates many of the same genes as retinol, supporting collagen and epidermal renewal, without acting through retinoid receptors. It also has antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial properties in lab studies.
Risks and caveats: Reviews say it lacks the burning and scaling commonly seen with topical retinoids, but one systematic review also notes a report of adverse events. Product labels advise avoiding eyes, stopping if irritation occurs and not applying to broken skin. It shows estrogen-receptor activity in lab studies, whose clinical meaning in skin products is not established.
deepLead:
Bakuchiol is a meroterpene phenol obtained mainly from the seeds of Psoralea corylifolia, a plant used in traditional Indian and Chinese medicine for conditions such as psoriasis and leprosy . It has become a cosmetic ingredient promoted as a 'retinol alternative' for photoaging, wrinkles, hyperpigmentation and acne .
Despite having no structural resemblance to retinoids, bakuchiol was reported in a 2014 study to regulate gene expression similarly to retinol . A 2019 randomized, double-blind trial in the British Journal of Dermatology compared topical bakuchiol with retinol for facial photoageing . A 2022 systematic review of 30 articles, 16 of them preclinical and seven clinical, concluded that results in photoaging, acne and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation were comparable to retinoids, while observing that the clinical evidence is small .

name: Mandelic acid

chain: Fewer clogged pores and dark spots
angle.text: Mandelic acid is a large-molecule alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums for acne, dark spots, acne marks and photoaging, often by people with sensitive skin. Direct clinical evidence is thin, with most support coming from related acids.

summary: A larger, slower-penetrating alpha-hydroxy acid used in gentle peels and serums for acne and dark spots; direct clinical evidence is thin.
note: Studied mostly as part of formulations or in broader AHA reviews; few dedicated trials of mandelic acid alone.
currentQuick:
Mandelic acid is an alpha-hydroxy acid (AHA) used in skincare as a chemical exfoliant, mainly for acne, uneven pigmentation and sensitive skin. It is sold in serums and professional-strength peels.
A large Cochrane review covered AHA treatments for acne as a class. Dedicated mandelic acid trials are limited in the available literature; registered trials compare mandelic peels with tranexamic acid for melasma and test a combined peel for periocular rejuvenation.
How it works: Mandelic acid is described as having a larger molecular size than glycolic acid, which is said to slow skin penetration and reduce irritation. As an AHA it promotes exfoliation and cell turnover, and encyclopedic summaries describe antibacterial activity.
Risks and caveats: Common AHA effects are stinging, redness and peeling. The published literature give little mandelic acid-specific safety data. It has been studied as a natural preservative in emulsions, and sun protection is generally advised with AHA products.
deepLead:
Mandelic acid (2-hydroxy-2-phenylacetic acid) is a chiral alpha-hydroxy acid with the formula C8H8O3 . In cosmetics and dermatology it is used as a chemical exfoliant for acne, hyperpigmentation and photoaging .
An encyclopedic summary says it penetrates skin more slowly than smaller AHAs such as glycolic acid because of its larger molecule, and therefore causes less irritation, and cites formulation studies reporting acne lesion reductions of up to 69% . That summary is AI-generated and its citations were not verified here.
Controlled clinical evidence specific to mandelic acid is sparse. A Cochrane review assessed topical alpha-hydroxy acids for acne as a group, and registered trials are examining mandelic peels in melasma and in a periocular peel .

name: Tea tree oil

angle.text: Tea tree oil is used topically for acne, post-shave breakouts, body odor and scalp care, and is sometimes claimed to lower testosterone. Small trials exist for acne and eyelid mites; the testosterone and shaving claims rest on anecdote.

summary: Australian essential oil with proven lab antimicrobial activity and small acne and eyelid-mite trials; widely used topically, with contact allergy and toxicity if swallowed.
note: Use diluted and externally only per labels; irritation and allergic contact dermatitis are documented, and swallowing is toxic.
currentQuick:
Tea tree oil is the essential oil distilled from the leaves of Melaleuca alternifolia, a tree native to eastern Australia. It is used in soaps, washes, gels and shampoos for acne, fungal skin conditions, body odor and eyelid cleansing.
In laboratory studies it has broad antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity. Human evidence is a mix of small pilot trials (for example, a 5% acne gel pilot with 18 people) and eyelid-mite studies; large trials for appearance outcomes are scarce.
How it works: Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, disrupts the membranes of bacteria and yeast in laboratory studies, and has been shown to suppress inflammatory mediators such as TNF-alpha and interleukins in activated human monocytes.
Risks and caveats: Reviews and dermatology references note irritation and allergic contact dermatitis; an encyclopedic summary reports reactions in a small percentage of users and toxicity if swallowed. Product labels advise external use only. Pure oil is generally used diluted.
deepLead:
Tea tree oil is an essential oil produced by steam distillation of Melaleuca alternifolia leaves, a plant native to eastern Australia, with terpinen-4-ol as its primary active component . A 2006 review describes it as used for almost 100 years in Australia and now sold worldwide as neat oil and as an ingredient in many products, chiefly for its antiseptic and anti-inflammatory properties .
Laboratory studies show broad antimicrobial activity against bacteria, yeast and fungi, and anti-inflammatory effects on human monocytes . Human trials include a pilot study of tea tree oil gel for acne, studies of its use against Demodex mites and blepharitis, and trials in oral care and wound-related uses .
Its main role in looksmaxxing-type contexts is as an acne and skin-care ingredient; forum mentions are sparse. Contact allergy and toxicity on ingestion are documented .

name: Squalane

angle.text: Squalane is a light moisturising oil used in serums and moisturisers, and on lips and hair, to leave skin soft and supple. The smoother, hydrated feel is immediate, though trial data specific to squalane is limited.

summary: Shelf-stable, lightweight moisturising oil made from squalene; widely used in skincare, with little trial data of its own.
note: Evidence for appearance benefits rests mostly on general emollient science and product descriptions, not squalane-specific trials.
currentQuick:
Squalane is a stable, oily hydrocarbon made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid that also occurs in human skin oil. It is sold as a lightweight moisturiser or ingredient in serums, facial oils and hair products.
It is described as non-greasy and suitable for many skin types, but those descriptions come largely from general references and cosmetic marketing. Few controlled trials have tested squalane on its own.
How it works: As an emollient and occlusive lipid it is thought to help the skin retain water; reviews report hydrating and emollient activity mainly from animal and laboratory work, and lipid-replacement studies in human skin show barrier lipids affect water-holding.
Risks and caveats: Reviewed sources describe low irritation potential and generally recommend patch testing for sensitive skin. It is a cosmetic ingredient sold over the counter. Sourcing differs between plant-derived and historically shark-derived material.
deepLead:
Squalane is a saturated hydrocarbon (C30H62) made by hydrogenating squalene, a lipid found in human sebum, shark liver oil, olives and some other plant sources. It is a colourless, odourless, lightweight oil used mainly as an emollient and skin-conditioning ingredient in moisturisers, serums and hair products.
In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a gentle, non-greasy moisturiser and as a vehicle in skincare products. Published research on squalane itself as a cosmetic active is sparse: most of the literature concerns squalene and squalane as vaccine adjuvant components, as drug-delivery vehicles and as skin-barrier lipids. One small randomised trial tested a fullerene-in-squalane cosmetic against wrinkles, but it did not isolate squalane's own effect.
Reviews describe emollient and skin-hydrating activity for squalene and squalane, largely from in vitro and animal work. Squalane is sold over the counter in cosmetic products and appears in some US-listed topical product labels.
